nameStory: The Atlantic black sea hare gets its name from its dark, sooty coloration and its rabbit-like appearance when viewed from above. The two rhinophores (sensory tentacles) on its head look remarkably like a hare's ears, giving this marine mollusk its endearing common name.
description: The Atlantic black sea hare is a fascinating sea slug that looks more like a dark, gelatinous blob than a typical snail. These soft-bodied marine animals can grow quite large, with their dark brown to black bodies having a smooth, almost rubbery texture. Unlike land snails, they have no external shell, though they do have small internal shell plates. Their most distinctive features are the two tentacle-like rhinophores on their head that really do resemble rabbit ears.

idTips.label: Rabbit-ear tentacles
idTips.description: Two prominent rhinophores stick up from the head like rabbit ears, constantly moving and tasting the water

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Body ranges from dark brown to jet black, sometimes with a sooty or mottled appearance

idTips.label: Soft, rubbery texture
idTips.description: Body feels smooth and gelatinous to the touch, like firm jello, with no hard shell visible

idTips.label: Wing-like flaps
idTips.description: Large parapodia (side flaps) extend from the body and can fold over the back like wings

idTips.label: Purple ink release
idTips.description: When disturbed, releases a cloud of dark purple ink that smells slightly fishy

habitat: Atlantic black sea hares prefer warm coastal waters and are more commonly found along the southern New England coast, particularly in shallow bays and tide pools during warmer months. They're typically spotted on rocky shores or sandy bottoms where seaweed and algae are abundant, as these form their primary food source.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters yet, as coastal temperatures are still too cool for these warm-water lovers.
seasonality.summer: Most likely to be spotted during the warmest summer months when ocean temperatures peak, often found grazing on seaweed in shallow areas.
seasonality.fall: May still be present in early fall if water temperatures remain warm, but become less active as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having moved to warmer southern waters or deeper areas offshore.

funFact: When threatened, sea hares can release up to 40 million purple ink particles per second, creating a smokescreen that not only hides them visually but also overwhelms predators' sense of smell - it's like throwing a stink bomb and smoke grenade at the same time!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark sea slugs or even jellyfish when floating. The key difference is those distinctive rabbit-ear rhinophores - no other marine animal in New England has that exact combination of dark color and prominent "ears" sticking up from the head.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name "sea hare," these animals are actually mollusks - they're more closely related to snails and clams than to any furry mammal. The "hare" name is purely based on appearance and has led to some confusion about what type of animal they actually are.
compareHints: As the only Aplysia species regularly found in New England waters, the Atlantic black sea hare is most easily compared to other sea slug families. Unlike nudibranchs which have colorful external gills, sea hares have their gills hidden under their wing-like flaps and tend to be much larger and darker in color.
